doc.title: Bob Cranshaw interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995

chapter: Church, energy and the state of jazz
title: The bass as a voice and listening to church choirs
summary: He wanted to sing bass; he listened to his father's church choir from the basement, and Woods notes other players' church-derived spiritual energy.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: So it’s a voice for you? The bass is a voice, isn’t it?

It is a voice. It is a football thing, you know. It’s the bottom, it’s the stability or whatever, you know the lineman is the linebacker, it’s that thing that holds the glue to the whole band, so I think in wanting to sing bass. But I’d listen to my father. I’d go in and I’d listen to the choir and I would go in the basement of the church and I would just sit downstairs and I would listen and I could hear the music. But the rhythms of all the people in the church and the thing, they would be burning. I mean it felt so good. That was the part that was really great to me that I liked. The feeling was just incredible.

You know I want to say, just make an interjection here and want you to come back on that a little bit. Many, many of the players we’ve interviewed so far have said that an initial energy, a sense of spirituality, not religiously, not in a pious way, but a sense of spiritual energy, they’ve gleaned from church. © Fillius Jazz Archive -12-
